corrected_value.authors: Gneezy U , Keenan EA , Gneezy A
corrected_value.title: Avoiding overhead aversion in charity

decisions.quote: Hypothesis 7, which found that participants were biased towards a charity where overhead is paid for by another donor even when cost-effectiveness is kept constant, acts as a conceptual replication of Gneezy et al . [ 16 ]. In contrast to the between-subject design that they used in their study, our extension shows that this effect occurs in a within-subject context as well.
decisions.reason: In Section 1.7.2 (External funding effect), Section 2.8.2, Section 3.3.2, and Section 4.2 (Extensions), the authors formulate and empirically test Hypothesis 7 across Studies 1 and 2 (combined N = 706), testing whether donors prefer a charity whose overhead costs are covered by another donor over a charity where donations pay for overhead when cost-effectiveness is held constant. In Section 4.2, the authors explicitly state that Hypothesis 7 acts as a conceptual replication of Gneezy et al. [16] (Gneezy, Keenan, & Gneezy, 2014, DOI 10.1126/science.1253932), contrasting Gneezy et al.'s between-subject design with their own within-subject design. The only shipped row (row 826) is Baron and Szymanska (2011, DOI 10.4324/9780203865972-24), which is a different original work that did not test externally funded overhead.
